description: We are a cross-disciplinary team working on harmonizing MODIS and VIIRS hot spot data. Using open NASA datasets, we aim to prototype a reproducible pipeline and visualization that reconciles sensor differences and delivers a more consistent fire hotspot product
summary:
FireHarmony is an interactive web application developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 to harmonize MODIS and VIIRS active fire detections. Because these sensors have different spatial resolutions (1 km vs. 375 m) and operational periods, their data cannot be simply merged. Our tool solves this by using an adjustable spatiotemporal matching algorithm. Users can define the maximum distance and time gap to merge detections of the same fire into unified clusters, ensuring a single, accurate event record while preserving unique single-sensor detections. 

The dashboard features a real-time map, a false-positive filter to exclude persistent heat sources (like industrial flares), and an "Anomaly Watch" that uses Z-score analysis to flag days with abnormally high fire activity. This project is crucial because it creates a more complete and reliable historical record of fires. It empowers researchers and fire managers to accurately compare current fire activity against historical norms, improving global climate monitoring and disaster response.
details:
What it does and how it works:

FireHarmony is a web application designed to unify active fire detections from the MODIS and VIIRS satellite sensors. Because these sensors differ in spatial resolution (1 km vs. 375 m), time of overpass, and detection algorithms, their raw data cannot be simply combined. Our application solves this by applying a greedy spatial-temporal matching algorithm. Through an interactive dashboard, users can adjust sliders to set the maximum distance (e.g., 1 km) and time gap (e.g., 3 hours). The algorithm uses grid-bucketing and the Haversine formula to rapidly identify and merge detections of the same fire into a single "harmonized" event, while preserving unique detections seen by only one sensor. The app also features a false-positive filter to exclude persistent heat sources (such as industrial flares) and an anomaly-detection system.

Benefits and Intended Impact:

The primary benefit is the creation of a single, clean, and complete historical record of global fire activity. By combining the long-term climate record of MODIS with the high-resolution sensitivity of VIIRS, FireHarmony eliminates blind spots that a single-sensor dataset would have. The intended impact is to empower researchers, climate scientists, and fire management agencies with a reliable tool to compare current fire activity against historical norms. By identifying "burning-activity calendars" and flagging anomalously high-fire days, our project supports improved disaster response, environmental monitoring, and climate trend analysis.

Tools, Languages, and Software:

Frontend: Vanilla JavaScript (ES6+), HTML5, CSS3, Leaflet.js (for interactive mapping), and Chart.js (for data visualization).

Backend (BFF): Node.js and Express.js (to securely proxy API requests, hide the NASA MAP_KEY, and handle CORS).

Data Source: NASA FIRMS API (Active Fire Data).

Tools: Visual Studio Code, Git/GitHub, npm.

(No specialized hardware was required; the app runs entirely in the browser).

How is it creative?

Instead of hardcoding a rigid rule (e.g., "always prioritize MODIS"), we made the harmonization process interactive and transparent. Users can physically drag sliders to see how changing the spatiotemporal parameters affects the data in real time. Furthermore, we included a statistical anomaly watch using Z-scores to highlight extreme fire days, and a false-positive filter that visually rings persistent hotspots (like volcanoes) so they aren't mistaken for wildfires. Finally, we built a built-in synthetic data fallback, ensuring the app never crashes during a presentation if the NASA API rate limit is reached.

Factors the Team Considered:

Performance: Comparing every MODIS point to every VIIRS point takes too long. We implemented a grid-bucketing spatial index to reduce the algorithmic complexity, allowing the sliders to update the map instantly.

Scientific Validity: We used the Haversine formula to calculate exact distances on Earth's curvature and accounted for the different confidence scales between the two sensors (numeric vs. low/nominal/high).

API Limitations: We designed a Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) to cache requests and handle the strict 5-day limit imposed by the NASA FIRMS API, preventing the frontend from failing.

User Experience: We added accessible tooltips, legends, and an intuitive layout so non-experts can understand complex satellite harmonization concepts.
dataRefs: NASA FIRMS (Fire Information for Resource Management System)
